description: Ayodhya, in Uttar Pradesh, holds a cluster of Jain shrines tied to Jain tradition, which counts the city as the birthplace of five Tirthankaras: Rishabhanatha (Adinath), Ajitanatha, Abhinandananatha, Sumatinatha and Anantanatha. A district government page says 18 kalyanaks (sacred life events of Tirthankaras) took place here. Several shrines mark these birthplaces; a district government page attributes five birthplace shrines to Kesari Singh, treasurer to the Nawab of Faizabad; the date of construction is not firmly established. The best-known complex is the Digambar Badi Murti temple in the Raiganj area, which enshrines a tall standing marble image of Rishabhadeva, with side altars to other Tirthankaras. Other sites include tonks, small memorials holding footprint images, such as Anantanatha's on the Sarayu bank, and an older temple in the Katra area. Several shrines have been rebuilt or newly built in recent years. Jain pilgrims treat Ayodhya as a tirtha because of these associations.

description: Bade Hanuman Mandir, also called Lete Hanuman Ji Mandir, stands near the Allahabad Fort and about a kilometre from the Triveni Sangam in Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh. Its principal image shows Hanuman in a reclining posture, which one government tourism page describes as set roughly 6 to 7 feet below ground level. According to Wikipedia, the idol becomes partly submerged when the Ganga floods during the monsoon. Local legend, as reported by Wikipedia, holds that a childless merchant from Kannauj had the image carved from Vindhya stone and that the ascetic Baba Balagiri Ji Maharaj later installed it here; the article dates the temple to about 700 years ago. Another tradition says that in 1582 the Mughal emperor Akbar tried to move the idol, failed, and instead built his fort wall behind the shrine. A separate account describes the image as about 20 feet long. Hanuman Jayanti and Ram Navami are among the festivals noted, and the Tuesdays of the Jyeshtha month, known as Bada Mangal, are reported to draw large crowds.

description: Banke Bihari Temple is a Krishna temple in Vrindavan, in Mathura district, Uttar Pradesh. According to Wikipedia, the deity was first worshipped at Nidhivan by the devotional singer Swami Haridas, who called it Kunj Bihari, and his disciples later named it Banke Bihari for its tribhanga, or three-bend, stance. The image is regarded as the joint form of Radha and Krishna and is worshipped as a child. A website maintained by the temple's sewa adhikaris (servitors) says the image was granted to Haridas by the divine couple at Nidhivan. The present building, raised by the goswami families who serve the deity, dates from the 1860s according to Wikipedia, after the image moved from Nidhivan in the nineteenth century. The temple is known for its darshan custom: a curtain is drawn across the deity every few minutes, so that viewing is intermittent. Tradition says an unbroken gaze would draw the deity away with the devotee. Bihar Panchami marks the appearance of the image, and Janmashtami is also observed. The temple's administration has been the subject of Supreme Court proceedings since 2025.

description: Ram Ghat is the main bathing ghat on the Mandakini river at Chitrakoot Dham, in Chitrakoot district, Uttar Pradesh. Chitrakoot is traditionally associated with Rama, Sita and Lakshmana, who, according to local belief reported by the district administration, lived in the area for roughly eleven years of their forest exile. The ghat has stepped banks lined with boats and is linked by tradition to the poet-saint Tulsidas, who is said to have had a vision of Rama here; the national tourism site adds that he composed the Ramcharitmanas on these banks, which is a traditional claim. Pilgrims bathe in the river before rituals, and an evening Mandakini aarti with lamps, bells and chanting is held on the riverbank. Nearby, the hill of Kamadgiri is the focus of a circumambulation of about five kilometres. Upstream on the river bank lies the Sphatik Shila, a small boulder noted on the district tourism page.

description: Devi Patan Temple is a Shakti shrine at Tulsipur, in Balrampur district, Uttar Pradesh, close to the border with Nepal. The goddess is worshipped as Maa Pateshwari, and the temple is counted by tradition among the Shakti Peethas. The usual legend is that a part of Sati's body fell here when Shiva carried it; accounts differ on which part, with the district website naming the shoulder and other pages saying right shoulder or right thigh. Local tradition also says the Siddha Peeth was founded by Guru Gorakhnath of the Nath sampradaya, that King Vikramaditya built the present shrine, and that King Suheldeo of Shravasti renovated it in the eleventh century. The Balrampur royal family is described as its caretaker. A pond called Surya Kund is said to have been made by Karna. Navratri brings large gatherings, and in Chaitra a procession (Shobha Yatra) of Pir Ratan Nath, brought from Dang in Nepal, joins the worship. Devotees also offer hair here.

description: Kampil, the ancient Kampilya, lies in Farrukhabad district of Uttar Pradesh, about 45 km west of the district headquarters. Wikipedia describes it as the capital of southern Panchala, ruled by King Drupada in the Mahabharata, and tradition places Draupadi's swayamvara here, where Arjuna is said to have won her hand by the fish-eye feat. The district administration's page says Draupadi Kund is believed to mark her manifestation and that the Rameshwarnath Shiva temple stands where, by local tradition, Shatrughna installed a linga on the Ganga's bank. The town is also revered in Jainism as the place linked to the four kalyanakas of the 13th Tirthankara, Vimalanatha, and both Shwetambar and Digambar temples stand here. The district page adds that the Chinese traveller Xuanzang and the archaeologist Alexander Cunningham recorded the town's historical importance. The town holds several separate shrines rather than a single temple.

description: The Durga Mandir stands beside the Durga Kund tank in the Durgakund and Bhelupur area of Varanasi. Wikipedia attributes its construction to Rani Bhabani, a Bengali queen of Natore, in the 18th century, with no firm date recorded; an Outlook Traveller feature gives 1760. It follows the North Indian Nagara style, with a cluster of small spires and a red-ochre exterior, and a hall of gold-trimmed columns. Wikipedia reports a local belief that the goddess's image manifested on its own, and cites the Devi Bhagavata Purana for a legend of a royal wedding and a war won with Durga's help; both are tradition, not documented history. The kund beside it was once linked to the Ganga, and has steps for ritual bathing. Durga Puja and Navratri are the main festival occasions. An Outlook Traveller feature links the temple to the long Bengali presence in Kashi's religious life.

description: The Gorakhnath Mandir, also called Gorakhnath Math, sits in the centre of Gorakhpur in eastern Uttar Pradesh, on a campus Wikipedia puts at about 52 acres. The city takes its name from Gorakhnath, a yogi of about the 11th century CE who travelled widely and whose writings belong to the Nath Sampradaya canon; the tradition itself is traced to his guru Matsyendranath. According to Wikipedia, a shrine was raised where Gorakhnath practised, with a chamber associated with his samadhi, halls for other deities and a room of the nine Naths. A flame is said by the temple tradition to have burned since his time. The complex also includes a goshala. Makar Sankranti is a major festival, when devotees offer khichdi to Gorakhnath. The math is led by a mahant. The district administration describes the grounds as a cultural hub, with an evening light and sound show.

description: The Govind Dev Ji temple in Vrindavan was built in red sandstone and is dated by Wikipedia and a Rana Safvi essay to 1590, when Raja Man Singh I of Amber completed it with the Vrindavan Goswamis during Akbar's reign, after roughly 14 years of work. Wikipedia says Rupa Goswami built the first permanent temple around 1535 and that Akbar donated the sandstone, and it also records a consecration in 1570; Safvi describes a turtle-shaped plan facing east with a vaulted hall on a Greek cross layout and a lotus frieze, echoing Fatehpur Sikri. Wikipedia describes the building as seven-storeyed. The Govindadeva image was removed from Vrindavan for safety in 1670, when Wikipedia says the town was sacked on Aurangzeb's orders, and was later installed in Jaipur, where it is worshipped today in Jaipur's Govind Dev Ji temple. The Vrindavan building survives, although Wikipedia, citing a historian, says its sanctuary was dismantled at that time. A 19th-century repair by F. S. Growse is mentioned by Safvi.

description: Hanuman Garhi is a fort-like Hanuman temple in Ayodhya, reached by a flight of 76 steps. Wikipedia describes it as shaped like a four-sided fort with circular ramparts at each corner, with silver carvings adorning the sanctum, and a roughly six-inch image of the child Hanuman seated on his mother Anjani's lap. Local tradition holds that this is where Hanuman stayed while guarding Ramkot. Wikipedia notes a Skanda Purana attribution of the first shrine to King Vikramaditya, and a travel guide places the present structure in the 18th century under the Nawabs of Awadh; accounts of the site's early history differ. Management rests with Ramanandi Bairagi mahants of the Nirvani Akhara. Festivals include Hanuman Jayanti, Ram Navami, Dussehra and Diwali, and Bada Mangal.

description: Hastinapur, in Meerut district of Uttar Pradesh, is a Jain pilgrimage centre regarded as the birthplace of three Tirthankaras: Shantinatha, Kunthunatha and Aranatha. Jain tradition also holds that Rishabhanatha ended a long fast here by accepting sugarcane juice from King Shreyans, an event Jains link to Akshaya Tritiya. The Digambar Bada Mandir, dedicated to Shantinatha and built on a small hillock, dates in its present form to 1801 according to Wikipedia, with consecration around 1806. The Bada Mandir has a 31-foot manastambha at its entrance and a Trimurti shrine with a Shantinatha image Wikipedia describes as 12th-century. Elsewhere in the town are the Jambudweep complex, founded by Gyanmati in 1972, a 131-foot Kailash Parvat dedicated to Rishabhanatha, the Ashtapad structure built by the Shwetambar teerth trust, and a Shwetambar Shantinatha temple. A Jain heritage site describes the tirth as served by both Shwetambar and Digambar committees, with dharamshalas and fairs on Kartik and Falgun Purnima and Vaishakh Sud 3.

description: Hastinapur is a town in Meerut district, Uttar Pradesh, on the right bank of the Ganga, roughly 37 km from Meerut city. The Mahabharata and Puranas present it as the capital of the Kuru kingdom. Archaeologist B.B. Lal excavated the site in the early 1950s, work that examined the Painted Grey Ware sequence and was linked by some to Mahabharata traditions. Today the name covers a cluster of shrines rather than a single temple. Pandeshwar Temple, a Shiva shrine, is traditionally associated with the education of the Kauravas and Pandavas, and local tradition holds that Yudhishthira installed its linga. The nearby Karna Temple has a Shivling traditionally credited to Karna; the present temple building is new. Hastinapur is also a significant Jain pilgrimage centre, with the Digambar Jain Bada Mandir, the Ashtapad Teerth, Kailash Parvat and Jambudweep complexes, and Sikhs honour it as the birthplace of Bhai Dharam Singh, one of the Panj Pyare, with a gurdwara nearby at Saifpur Karamchandpur.

description: Kanak Bhawan, sometimes called the Golden Palace, is a Rama and Sita temple in Ayodhya, Uttar Pradesh, in the north-east of the Ramkot area. According to tradition, Queen Kaikeyi gave the palace to Sita after her marriage to Rama. The present building dates from 1891, when Maharani Vrishabhan Kunwari of Orchha and Tikamgarh, together with her husband, rebuilt it. Its style is said to resemble the palaces of Bundelkhand and Rajasthan, and it was built to look more like a royal palace than a conventional shrine. The sanctum holds three pairs of Rama and Sita images. The largest is attributed to the Maharani, a smaller pair is traditionally linked to King Vikramaditya, and the smallest is believed to have been given by Krishna to a woman devotee. Ram Navami and Janaki Navami are its major festivals. Sources differ on earlier dates and builders.

description: Kashi Vishwanath Temple stands in Vishwanath Gali on the western bank of the Ganga in Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh. Its presiding deity is Shiva as Vishwanath or Vishweshwara, and it is counted among the twelve Jyotirlinga shrines. Wikipedia describes the linga as about 60 cm tall, set in a silver altar. The original shrine is recorded as destroyed in 1194, and later temples on or near the site were demolished in turn, with several historical accounts attributing a 1669 demolition order to Aurangzeb, after which the Gyanvapi Mosque was built on the site. Questions about the mosque and worship at its complex remain before the courts. The present temple was built next to the mosque in 1780 by Maharani Ahilyabai Holkar of Indore. Maharaja Ranjit Singh later donated gold for plating its spire and domes, which is why it is popularly called the Golden Temple. Since 1983 the temple has been managed by a board of trustees set up by the Uttar Pradesh government. The Kashi Vishwanath Corridor, linking it to the river, was inaugurated in December 2021.

description: The Krishna Janmasthan temple complex in Mathura, Uttar Pradesh, marks the place that Hindu tradition holds as the birthplace of Krishna, said to be the prison cell of Devaki and Vasudeva. Excavations at the site have found pottery and terracotta from about the 6th century BCE, and an inscription dated 1150 records a Vishnu temple there. Accounts say the Keshavdeva temple was destroyed in 1670 and the Shahi Idgah mosque built on its plinth, and the mosque still stands beside the complex. The land passed through British auction in the early 19th century to Raja Patnimal's family. In 1944 Madan Mohan Malaviya bought it, with funds from Jugal Kishore Birla. A trust, now the Shri Krishna Janmasthan Seva Sansthan, was registered in 1951. The present Keshavdeva temple and Bhagavata Bhavan were built between 1953 and 1982. The 1968 agreement between the trust and the Idgah committee, and the ownership of the Idgah land, are disputed in suits pending before the Allahabad High Court and the Supreme Court; as of late 2026 no final ruling has been reported, and the mosque's side contests the temple-side claims.

description: The Mahaparinirvana Temple, also called the Parinirvana Stupa, stands in Kushinagar in Kushinagar district of Uttar Pradesh. Buddhist tradition holds that Gautama Buddha passed into parinirvana here, and his cremation is traditionally placed at the nearby Ramabhar stupa. The shrine houses a reclining Buddha about 6.1 metres long, carved from a single block of sandstone, lying on his right side with the head to the north. Accounts say Ashoka is reported to have raised stupas at the site and that in the Gupta period the stupa was enlarged, the temple rebuilt and the large reclining image added. The broken image was excavated in the nineteenth century and restored by the Archaeological Survey of India, and the present temple was built by the Government of India in 1956 to mark 2,500 years of the Mahaparinirvana. A copper plate found in the excavations is reported to record that a donor named Haribala deposited it at the stupa. Today the site, with its lawns, excavated monastery ruins and circumambulation path, draws Buddhist pilgrims from many countries.

description: Naimisharanya, also called Nimsar or Nimkhar, is a sacred forest-tract on the left bank of the Gomati in Sitapur district, Uttar Pradesh, near Misrikh and about 32 km from Sitapur town. description: Sankat Mochan Hanuman Temple stands in southern Varanasi near the Assi river and is dedicated to Hanuman in his aspect as reliever of troubles. description: The Dhamekh Stupa rises in the Deer Park at Sarnath, roughly 8 km north-east of Varanasi, at the place where, in Buddhist tradition, the Buddha gave his first teaching to five former companions after his enlightenment. In July 2026 the UNESCO World Heritage Committee inscribed the Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath, of which the Dhamekh Stupa is part of the archaeological remains.

description: Varanasi is regarded in Jain tradition as the birthplace of four Tirthankaras, and the city's Jain sites are tied to them. description: Bhojeshwar Temple stands in Bhojpur village, Raisen district, Madhya Pradesh, about 28 km from Bhopal, and is dedicated to Shiva. The Archaeological Survey of India protects the monument. Thousands of devotees gather here at Maha Shivaratri, when the state government also holds the Bhojpur Utsav cultural event.

description: Deur Kothar (also spelled Deorkothar) is a Buddhist archaeological site near Teonthar in the Rewa region of Madhya Pradesh (listed under Rewa district by Wikipedia and Madhya Pradesh Tourism; district boundaries changed in 2023). According to Wikipedia it was discovered in 1982 by P.K. Mishra of the Archaeological Survey of India together with the village sarpanch Ajit Singh. The site has four brick stupa mounds, of which two were excavated; the largest stands about 9 metres high. Remains of roughly 30 further stupas in stone or brick survive, and the surrounding area has 63 rock shelters, some with old paintings and Brahmi inscriptions. A six-line Brahmi inscription on a pillar records that it was set up and dedicated to the Buddha, and names a teacher, Dharamdev, and his disciples. Tourism sources suggest a Mauryan date for the stupas, and Madhya Pradesh Tourism says they are believed to date from Ashoka's reign. The site was declared a monument of national importance in 1988 and the ASI carried out excavations in 1999-2000.

description: Dharmarajeshwara (Dharmrajeshwar) is a rock-cut temple site in Mandsaur district, Madhya Pradesh, near Chandwasa village and roughly 100 km from Mandsaur city. description: Jatashankar is a natural cave shrine dedicated to Shiva, set in a deep ravine in the Satpura hills near Pachmarhi in Madhya Pradesh, beneath large overhanging rocks. According to regional tradition, this is where Shiva took refuge from the demon Bhasmasura. Wikipedia also notes a cold spring-fed pond and a hot one in the surrounding area. The cave is listed among the sights of Pachmarhi by Madhya Pradesh Tourism; no firm date for the shrine is established.

description: Kalinjar is a hill fort on a rocky outcrop at the eastern end of the Vindhya range in Banda district, Uttar Pradesh, in the Bundelkhand region. The fort stands about 367 metres above sea level. Its best-known shrine is the Neelkanth temple, dedicated to Shiva. According to the legend associated with it, Shiva drank the poison produced at the churning of the ocean, turning his throat blue, and then came to Kalinjar and overcame Kal, time or death, which is said to explain the name. The Chandela dynasty, which expanded the fort, used the title Kalanjaradhipati, lord of Kalinjar. Historical accounts record Mahmud of Ghazni's attack in 1023 and British annexation in 1812, with the fort passing through several rulers in between. The fort is now in ruins.

description: The Jain temples of Khajuraho lie in the eastern part of the town, an area where Jains appear to have lived during the Chandela period. The three best-known shrines, Parshvanatha, Adinatha and Shantinatha, stand inside a compound wall dated to the early twelfth century. An inscription dates the Parshvanatha temple to 954 CE, naming its builder Pahila and the Chandela king Dhanga. The same temple holds an early magic square, the Chautisa Yantra, a 4x4 magic square in which every row, column and diagonal sums to 34. The Adinatha idol carries an inscription of 1027, during Madanavarman's reign. The Shantinatha temple is a later composite built partly from older temple remains; its main idol of the sixteenth Tirthankara is described as about 15 feet tall in one source and 14 feet in another, and bears an inscription equivalent to 1028 CE. Incredible India also lists a Ghantai temple in the group. The Khajuraho complex is a UNESCO World Heritage Site covering both Hindu and Jain monuments.

description: Khajuraho, in Chhatarpur district of Madhya Pradesh, was a capital of the Chandela dynasty between roughly the ninth and twelfth centuries. Historical accounts suggest about 85 temples were built by the twelfth century; roughly 20 survive (counts vary, UNESCO notes 23) across some six square kilometres, in Western, Eastern and Southern groups. Most were built between about 950 and 1050 CE. The Kandariya Mahadeva, dedicated to Shiva and credited to King Ganda between 1017 and 1029, has a spire about 116 feet high and over 870 sculptures. The Lakshmana temple is dedicated to Vishnu and the Vishvanatha to Shiva, completed in 999. Alongside Hindu shrines, the Eastern Group has Jain temples. Erotic scenes form roughly ten percent of the carvings; most depict daily life, mythology and symbolic themes. Scholars differ on their meaning: some connect them to Tantric practice, while others see them as expressing the place of kama in Hindu life. UNESCO inscribes the Khajuraho Group of Monuments as a World Heritage Site.

description: Kundalpur, in Damoh district of Madhya Pradesh and about 37 km from Damoh city, is a major Digambar Jain pilgrimage centre, also called Kundalgiri. The principal image is a seated Rishabhanatha, the first Tirthankara, known as Bade Baba or Adinath, about 15 feet tall. Nineteenth-century surveyors misidentified it as Neminatha and Mahavira; later work established it as Rishabhanatha. The old temple is estimated to date from the 6th to 8th century by different accounts, and an inscription of 1700 CE records renovation by disciples of Bhattaraka Surendrakirti with help from the Bundela ruler Chhatrasal. Alexander Cunningham counted about 20 temples on the hill and 30 at its foot in 1884, while a Jain pilgrimage site lists 64 temples. Tradition links the hill with the liberation of Shridhar Kevali, the last Kevali. In 2006 the main image was shifted into a large new temple built under the inspiration of Acharya Vidyasagar.

description: Mahakaleshwar is a Shiva temple on the bank of the Shipra river in Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh, and one of the twelve Jyotirlingas. Its lingam is regarded as swayambhu, self-manifested, and faces south, a feature the Ujjain district website describes as found only here among the twelve Jyotirlingas, according to tantric tradition. The sanctum is part of a multi-level complex that includes an Omkareshwar shrine above it, images of Ganesh, Parvati and Karttikeya, and a Nagchandreshwar idol opened for darshan only on Nag Panchami. Legend tells of King Chandrasena and a boy, Shrikhar, whose prayers brought Shiva to protect Ujjain in the form of Mahakala. Wikipedia records destruction of the older complex in 1234-35 and reconstruction in the eighteenth century under Maratha rule. The Bhasma Aarti is held at dawn, around 4 a.m.; the ash was traditionally said to come from funeral pyres, but is now reportedly prepared from cow dung. The temple is administered under the Ujjain district administration; a 2021 press report describes the Mahakaleshwar Temple Management Committee as chaired by the district collector.

description: Maheshwar is a temple town on the Narmada river in Khargone district of Madhya Pradesh. It is identified with the ancient Mahishmati, which the Ramayana and Mahabharata mention. In the 18th century Rajmata Ahilyabai Holkar, who succeeded Malhar Rao Holkar, made it the capital of her domain and is remembered for her religious and charitable works, including the rebuilt Kashi Vishwanath temple of 1780. About 2 km of the riverfront is stone-paved with some 28 ghats, among them Ahilya, Peshwa, Phanse and Mahila ghats, and Ahilya Ghat is the main starting point for boat rides. A fort-palace stands on the hill above the river with a Shiva shrine inside. Shiva temples in the town include Kaleshwar, Rajrajeshwar and Jwaleshwar. Maheshwar is also known for handloom Maheshwari saris, a craft that, according to one tourism account, was revived in 1979 through the Rehwa Society. The old temple town is best understood as a cluster of shrines and ghats rather than one single sanctum.

description: The Maa Sharda temple at Maihar stands on Trikuta (Trikut) hill and enshrines the goddess Sharda, regarded as a form of Saraswati. In Shakta tradition the shrine is counted among the Shakti Peethas, with the belief that Sati's necklace fell here; the town's name is also linked to that legend. Pilgrims reach the top by climbing about 1,063 steps (one source gives 1,064) or by ropeway. Local tradition holds that the brothers Alha and Udal, devotees of the goddess, found the shrine in the forest and that Alha still offers worship at dawn. Wikipedia dates the temple to around 502 CE, and one site mentions a Vikram Samvat 559 inscription on the image; these dates are traditional and should be treated cautiously. Other deities are also worshipped on the hilltop, and Navratri draws especially large crowds. Maihar is also known as the home of the Maihar gharana of Hindustani music, associated with Allauddin Khan.

description: Muktagiri, also called Mendhagiri, is a Digambar Jain pilgrimage site (siddha kshetra) in Bhainsdehi tehsil of Betul district, Madhya Pradesh, close to the Maharashtra border and reported to be about 14 km from Paratwada in Amravati district. description: Omkareshwar is one of the twelve Jyotirlinga shrines of Shiva, standing on the northern bank of the Narmada on Mandhata island (Shivpuri) in Khandwa district of Madhya Pradesh. description: The Chaturbhuj Temple at Orchha stands just outside the fort complex, near the Ram Raja Temple, in Orchha. Wikipedia says the Bundela rulers of Orchha built it in the 16th century: Madhukar Shah began it and his son Vir Singh Deo finished it. Local tradition holds that Queen Ganesh Kunwari, a devotee of Rama, brought an image of Rama from Ayodhya and kept it in her palace; when it was time to shift it here the image would not move, so the palace became the Ram Raja Temple and this temple's sanctum was left without that image. Wikipedia describes a cruciform plan, lotus decoration and tall pine-cone-shaped spires on a high platform, reached by a steep flight of steps, and the name Chaturbhuj means 'four-armed'. Wikipedia reports that an image of Radha Krishna is worshipped inside today. Wikipedia says the Ram Raja Trust handles day-to-day management, while the State Archaeology Department handles conservation of the structure.

description: The Siddhachal Caves are part of the Jain rock-cut sculptures cut into the cliffs around Gwalior Fort in Madhya Pradesh. Wikipedia says Babur recorded in his memoirs that he ordered the Urvai statues destroyed, while Sahapedia says the defacement is generally attributed to him; many figures were defaced. description: Sonagiri is a Digambara Jain pilgrimage site (siddha kshetra) in Datia district, Madhya Pradesh, roughly 65 km from Gwalior. description: Gurdwara Bangla Sahib is a major Sikh house of worship near Connaught Place in New Delhi, remembered for its association with Guru Har Krishan, the eighth Sikh Guru. The site was originally a bungalow of Raja Jai Singh of Amber, where the young Guru is said to have stayed during his visit to Delhi at a time when smallpox was spreading in the city. description: Gurdwara Rakab Ganj Sahib stands near Parliament House in New Delhi, on the site Sikh tradition identifies with the cremation of Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Sikh Guru, who was executed in Chandni Chowk in 1675. description: Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib is a historic Sikh shrine on Chandni Chowk in Old Delhi, marking the place where Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Sikh Guru, was beheaded in 1675 on the orders of Emperor Aurangzeb. The site once held the Mughal Kotwali, a police post and jail, where the Guru is said to have been held. description: Purana Qila, the Old Fort, in central Delhi is a 16th-century citadel that tradition links with Indraprastha, the Pandava capital of the Mahabharata. The fort itself is historically documented: the Delhi government's heritage portal says Humayun founded it in 1533 as the inner citadel of his city Din-Panah, and Sher Shah Suri, who took it in 1540, renamed it Shergarh and built the Qila-i-Kuhna mosque and Sher Mandal. Archaeological Survey of India excavations, first led by B.B. Lal in 1954-55, found Painted Grey Ware in deeper levels of the mound. Lal and some ASI officials connect this pottery with the Mahabharata period, though Vasant Swarnkar, superintending archaeologist of the ASI's Delhi Circle, has said that the pottery from the 1954 dig was not found in a stratified deposit, so the identification with Indraprastha remains a hypothesis rather than an established fact. Excavations also revealed a long sequence of occupation from the Mauryan to Mughal periods.

description: Sri Digambar Jain Lal Mandir stands opposite the Red Fort in Chandni Chowk, Old Delhi. The temple is traditionally dated to 1656, in Shah Jahan's reign (some sources say 1658), when Jain officers of the Mughal army gathered around a tirthankara image kept in a tent; the present buildings date from 1878. Accounts differ on the principal icon, naming Parshvanatha or Mahavira, and an image of Rishabhanatha is also enshrined here. A manastambha column fronts the temple, and the first-floor prayer hall is topped by three red sandstone spires. Mahavir Jayanti is among the festivals observed. Behind the temple, the Jain Bird Hospital (Charity Birds Hospital) treats injured birds free of charge, reflecting the Jain principle of compassion for all living beings. It is reported to have begun in 1930 and to have moved into its present building in 1957, and its own figure is around 15,000 birds treated a year. The nearest metro station is Lal Qila.

description: Swaminarayan Akshardham in New Delhi is a temple complex built by the BAPS Swaminarayan Sanstha and consecrated by Pramukh Swami Maharaj on 6 November 2005. The main mandir is dedicated to Bhagwan Swaminarayan and, according to the BAPS site, is about 141 feet high, built in carved stone in a traditional style without ferrous metal, and houses over two hundred murtis. description: Yogmaya Temple is in Mehrauli, South Delhi, close to the Qutb complex, and is dedicated to the goddess Yogmaya. Tradition identifies her as a sister of Krishna, who in the Bhagavata story was exchanged with him at birth and warned the tyrant Kansa of his end. Local tradition, as reported by Wikipedia, holds that it is a pre-Sultanate shrine that was destroyed under the Mamluks and later restored; the present temple dates from 1827, when, according to heritage-walk accounts, Seth Sidha Mal of Chandni Chowk rebuilt it during the reign of Akbar II. Local belief also credits the Pandavas with founding it, which is not historically established. The main image is of black stone, and the shrine is busy during Navratri. The temple is central to Phool Walon Ki Sair, a three-day autumn festival, said to date from 1812, which begins at the nearby dargah of Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki and includes offering a floral fan to the goddess at this temple.

description: The Bhima Devi Temple Site Museum is an archaeological site and open-air museum at Pinjore in Panchkula district, Haryana, beside the Yadavindra (Pinjore) Gardens. It preserves the remains of a temple complex thought to have followed the Panchayatana plan of the Gurjara-Pratihara era, dated by Wikipedia to roughly the 8th to 12th century and by Haryana Tourism to about the 9th to 11th century. Excavations in 1974 exposed plinths and over a hundred sculptures. Because most carvings relate to Shiva, archaeologists have conjectured the principal deity was Shiva, while the name Bhima Devi points to a Shakti tradition. Surviving figures include Shiva, Parvati, Ganesha, Vishnu, Surya, the guardians of the directions, and Jain tirthankaras, along with musicians, apsaras and erotic reliefs that gave rise to the nickname Khajuraho of North India. Haryana Tourism says the complex was ruined over several centuries, with its final destruction linked to Aurangzeb's reign. The site is a protected monument.

description: Hemkund Sahib is a Sikh gurdwara beside the glacial Hemkund (Lokpal) lake in Chamoli district, Uttarakhand, at about 4,329 metres, ringed by seven peaks. description: Kalpeshwar is a small stone Shiva shrine in the Urgam valley of Chamoli district, Uttarakhand, at roughly 2,200 metres. It is the fifth and last temple of the Panch Kedar circuit. Its deity is Goddess Yamuna, whose image is carved from black stone; Incredible India describes her as the daughter of the sun god and twin sister of Yama. The temple stands at roughly 3,235 to 3,293 metres, depending on the source. Accounts of its origins differ: Incredible India says the Garhwal king Sudarshan Shah built it in 1839 and that Maharani Gularia Devi of Jaipur rebuilt it in the 19th century after an earthquake destroyed it, while Wikipedia gives Sudarshan Shah in one passage and Pratap Shah of Tehri in another. Beside the temple is Surya Kund, a hot spring where pilgrims cook rice and potatoes to offer to the goddess, and the Divya Shila rock is worshipped before the deity. Wikipedia places Janki Chatti about 7 km away. During winter the idol is moved to Kharsali for worship.
